answer.rationale: The revision answers the three concrete requests from R1. It adds a sample-size rationale, per-variable normality checks and an SDT-based theoretical implications section. R2 asked for no actionable changes. The visible changes are mostly added text, however, and Results, Tables 3–6, the Abstract and the Conclusions are almost unchanged. Several statistical reporting errors that bear directly on the core claims remain. First, a p value is reported as a t value and df = 2 is used for an independent-samples t test. Second, the fitness-page comparison has a 95% CI that includes 0 and a two-tailed Sig. of 0.120, yet the text and Abstract call it significant. Third, Table 5 reports F = 11.268 with p = 0.018, which do not match. The newly added sample-size and normality text introduces fresh inconsistencies: a 10% margin of error does not give 212, a 'normally distributed' independent variable sex is reported, and N is given as 211. The self-developed social comparison scale has only face validity, and its score range is wrong. The new theoretical implications extrapolate beyond the data. Only one sex-difference result is preserved at its original strength, and parts of the conclusions do not follow from the evidence. Substantive revision is therefore still needed.

issues.issue: Core inferential statistics are misreported, and the significance of some secondary findings is wrong. The p value is written as the t value and df = 2. Table 4 has a two-tailed Sig. of 0.120 and a 95% CI that includes 0, yet the result is declared significant. The Abstract still states that participants who follow fitness pages have more body image concerns. Table 5 reports F(2, ~209) = 11.268 with p = 0.018, which is numerically inconsistent.
issues.response_claim: Neither reviewer raised this point. R1 even judged 'If applicable, is the statistical analysis and its interpretation appropriate? Yes', and the authors made no response.
issues.observed_change: The Results text and Tables 3–5 in the revision are identical to the original manuscript. The Abstract conclusion is unchanged.

evidence.observation: In Table 4 of the revision, the two-tailed Sig. is 0.120 and the 95% CI runs from -0.84 to 7.22. The text instead uses the Levene Sig. of 0.028 as the basis for significance. In Table 3, df is uniformly 2.
Table 5 of the revision gives N = 63/60/89, F = 11.268 and Sig. = 0.018, which is inconsistent with the F distribution.

issues.issue: The normality test reporting is internally contradictory. The independent variable sex is described as normally distributed. Exercise motivation is not named, but Shapiro–Wilk p < 0.001 is attributed to an unnamed variable. N is given as 211, against a sample of 212. Results still repeats the old wording.

issues.observed_change: Data analysis gains a paragraph reporting SW, Q-Q plots and skewness/kurtosis for body image and social comparison. The third variable is not named. The Results section still says 'The data was normally distributed with Shapiro-Wilk statistic being 0.845'.

issues.issue: The sample-size rationale is not credible, and generalisation is limited. A 95% confidence level with a 10% margin of error does not yield 212. The claim that the sample can 'detect moderate effect sizes' comes with no power analysis. The sample is a convenience sample drawn mainly from friends and family, yet the limitations section calls it purposive.

issues.observed_change: Several sentences of qualitative justification were added after the existing calculation. No effect size, α, power or calculation formula is given, and the original calculation sentence is unchanged.

issues.issue: Measurement validity is weak. The social comparison scale was written by the authors and has only face validity. No reliability or structural validity in this sample is reported. The stated score range is wrong: the minimum of a 10-item 1–5 scale is 10, not 5, and the BSIQ minimum is likewise not 5. No internal consistency is reported for any of the three scales in this sample.

issues.issue: The new theoretical and practical implications go beyond the data. The study only compares sex differences cross-sectionally. It has no Instagram-use exposure contrast, and Table 6 reports men only. Even so, the paper uses causal wording such as 'how Instagram use affects'. It also draws gender-specific intrinsic versus extrinsic motivation conclusions from the SDT literature and recommends interventions such as parental psychoeducation. It further asserts that the cited review 'particularly focuses on sex differences', which cannot be verified here.

issues.observed_change: A 'Theoretical implications' section and practical-implication paragraphs were added. The Conclusions and the causal wording in the Discussion are unchanged.

evidence_limits: I did not access the OSF raw data, the scale validation PDF or the STROBE flow figure, so I could not recompute the t, F or p values. The inconsistency findings rest only on internal arithmetic consistency within the manuscript, such as CIs including 0 and the relation between F and p.
The Teixeira et al. (2012) source was not consulted, so whether it 'particularly focuses on sex differences' can only be flagged as unverifiable or questionable.
Which dependent variable the normality result with SW p < 0.001 belongs to is not stated in the manuscript. I can only infer that it is probably exercise motivation.
answer.process_consistency_auxiliary: Both reviewers were broadly positive, and R1 judged the statistical analysis appropriate. However, the materials show obvious statistical reporting errors that the reviewers did not identify. The author responses claim the issues were 'addressed', but the visible changes are limited to added text, and the core results tables are unchanged.
